question: What is the primary focus of the study of anatomy?

options.A: The electrical signals traveling through nerves
options.B: The physical structures and shapes of body parts
options.C: The chemical reactions inside living cells
options.D: The ways organs change when a person has a disease

explanation: Anatomy specifically looks at the physical structures, forms, and relative positions of body parts rather than how they function. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T1#GNS111_U1_T1_h1)

question: Why do nurses study anatomy and physiology together?

options.A: Pathology cannot occur without simultaneous changes in both areas
options.B: How an organ is built directly shapes how it does its job
options.C: Medical equipment is built based strictly on anatomical dimensions
options.D: It is a strict requirement for passing hospital licensing exams

explanation: You've got this! Structure and function always go hand in hand. An organ's physical shape is specially designed to make its everyday job possible. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T1#GNS111_U1_T1_h1)

question: What is the basic living unit of the human body?
explanation: Cells are recognized as the smallest independent living units that make up all human tissues and organs. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T1#GNS111_U1_T1_h2)

question: What is an organ made of?

options.A: Individual atoms bonded tightly into complex organic molecules
options.B: A collection of identical cells performing the exact same task
options.C: Two or more different types of tissues working together
options.D: Multiple organ systems functioning inside a single body cavity

explanation: Think of an organ like a team! It takes different tissue types working together—like muscle and lining tissues—to get a big job done. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T1#GNS111_U1_T1_h2)

question: What do we call all the chemical reactions that happen inside the body?
explanation: Great job! Metabolism is just the word we use for all the building up and breaking down of substances happening inside your cells to keep you going. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T1#GNS111_U1_T1_h3)

question: Which life process helps the body sense changes around it and react?
explanation: Responsiveness is your body's alert system! It's how you detect things like heat, cold, or pain and react quickly to stay safe. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T1#GNS111_U1_T1_h3)

question: How are the palms positioned in the standard anatomical position?
explanation: Remember, in standard anatomical position, you stand straight with your arms at your sides and your palms facing forward so the thumbs point away from the body. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T1#GNS111_U1_T1_h4)

question: A doctor looks at a scan that cuts the body horizontally into upper and lower parts. Which plane is this?
explanation: You're doing great! A transverse plane cuts across the body horizontally, giving us upper (superior) and lower (inferior) views. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T1#GNS111_U1_T1_h4)

question: Which major body cavity contains both the heart and the lungs?
explanation: The thoracic cavity is located in the upper chest and houses the lungs, heart, and major blood vessels. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T1#GNS111_U1_T1_h5)

question: What is the main job of the fluid inside serous membranes?

options.A: To supply oxygen directly to outer tissue layers
options.B: To regulate the internal temperature of abdominal organs
options.C: To reduce friction between moving organs and cavity walls
options.D: To trap invading bacteria and fight localized infections

explanation: Think of this fluid as a natural lubricant. It helps hardworking organs like your beating heart and expanding lungs glide smoothly without rubbing. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T1#GNS111_U1_T1_h5)

question: What is the primary goal of homeostasis in the human body?

options.D: Preventing all exposure to external bacteria

explanation: Homeostasis keeps vital internal conditions like temperature, blood pressure, and chemical balance within a safe, stable range. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T1#GNS111_U1_T1_h6)

question: Which of these is a classic example of a negative feedback loop?

options.C: Rapidly nursing an infant to increase milk flow
options.D: Forming a hard blood clot over a skin wound

explanation: Sweating is a classic negative feedback response. When you get too hot, your body works to cool you down, bringing things back to normal! [learn more](GNS111_U1_T1#GNS111_U1_T1_h6)
